1.א: [SA 1] The Tur rules that one who cooks on Shabbat is liable. The Beit Yosef (Kelal Gadol, 3a–1a) classifies bishul as one of the principal (av) melakhot; the Shulchan Aruch does not repeat it in this siman because the liability is self-evident.
1.ב: Baking bread, cooking food, steeping herbs, and heating water are all one category. Rambam, Hil. Shabbat 9:1: the measure for heating water is enough to bathe a small limb; for herbs, until they are fit for the use for which they are normally cooked. Rambam 9:6: heating any kind of metal, or heating metal until it forms a “glowing coal,” is a toladata of bishul; the same for heating wax, milk, tar, pitch, sulfur, and the like. Firing earthenware until it becomes pottery is bishul. In short, whether a hard body is softened by fire or a soft body hardened, one is liable for bishul. Cited: Magen Avraham.
1.ג: Meat on coals: if a kezayit’s worth is roasted (a third of a beitzah; see below OC 318:3, Mishnah Berurah), even in two or three places, one is liable. If that amount is not roasted but the piece is “half-cooked” throughout (see OC 253:28), one is liable. If it is only half-cooked on one side, he is exempt until he turns it and it is half-cooked on two sides. Rambam 9:5; Magen Avraham. The Ra’avad (as brought there) is discussed; Ateret Zekenim OC 9 shows that the Ra’avad still agrees with the Rambam on this. For chatat liability this is the rule, but for issur, many hold that even “half a measure” is forbidden mideorayta (Shabbat 74a, Rashi; Yoma 74a, R. Yochanan vs. Resh Lakish; we follow R. Yochanan). Kenesset HaGedolah in Beit Yosef YD 98:67 marshals sugyot that “half a measure” is assur mideorayta.
1.ד: A pot on the fire that would not be ready to finish cooking for an hour or two, and he turns the coals so that it cooks sooner—Ritva: it is possible he is liable. Pitchei Teshuvah 1. It would seem that, apart from the distinct issurim of extinguishing and kindling, R. Yonatan would still find a bishul liability here.
1.ה: Any case that is a matter of dispute whether it is “cooking” or not: the safek is treated as a Rabbinic safek, lekula. Ateret Zekenim 19. R. Yonatan: the stringency in bishul (and other melakhot) for mezid and shogeg is essentially a kenas; therefore we are lenient in safek. See below §8.
1.ו: Rema: “or if he did one of the other melakhot.” Netiv Chayim: this added line is a “mishnah she’einah tzricha,” for the Tur follows R. Meir, but we follow R. Yehudah and do not distinguish bishul from the other melakhot. So too Mishnah Berurah 1.
1.ז: The same Rema. If the action is only midrabbanan, Mishnah Berurah 1 forbids benefit even when done shogeg on that same day—because it is still a rabbinic melakhah. However, Gra elaborates that according to most opinions, if one violated only a rabbinic melakhah be‑shogeg, bedieved one does not forbid benefiting from it that same day (see Chayei Adam, kelal 9:11). But if done be‑mezid it is forbidden even to others until Motza’ei Shabbat (Chayei Adam there). If fruit was carried beyond the tehum and returned—even be‑mezid—it may be eaten that day, since the prohibition does not inhere in the fruit itself (OC 325:9).
1.ח: “Be‑mezid, forbidden to him forever”: meaning forbidden to benefit from that specific melakhah; proceeds from selling what was produced are permitted (Bava Kama 94a, Ketubot 34a; Chullin 116a and Rashi—it is only a penalty). There is a difficulty with Levush who writes “from the Torah”; see Ateret Zekenim 2 and Pitchei Teshuvah 1. Even permitted proceeds should reflect only the item’s pre‑melakhah value so that one does not profit from Shabbat labor.
1.ט: Same gloss: “forever” suggests (per Rashba §175) the pot may also be forbidden because absorbed taste belongs to “Ma’achal Ben Drusai.” Magen Avraham 1; Ateret Zekenim 1; Teshuvah Me’ahavah 1. Machatzit HaShekel disputes Magen Avraham and permits the pot; Arukh HaShulchan 1 agrees for another reason. R”Z 1 is stringent like Magen Avraham; Ben Ish Hai Beshalach 1 and later poskim likewise. Hagalah is effective even for earthenware; without hagalah one requires sixty against absorption—stricter than ordinary Gentile cooking (Ateret Zekenim 1, citing Levush YD 113—hagalah for cheres requires threefold koshering per YD 113:16).
1.י: If a Jew cooks for a dangerously ill patient, all agree the pot remains permitted (Rashba there; Machatzit HaShekel; Hagahos Taz). Even if the physician insists on a brand‑new pot (Shevus Yaakov YD 21).
1.יא: Same: household members are bound by the same prohibition against benefiting from the forbidden melakhah (Nachalas Shivah 1). If the violator dies the penalty may extend to his heir afterward—Magna Avraham names and Rema; Teshuvah Me’ahavah in this siman 1.
1.יב: Food cooked “for him”: halakhah follows others since it is not his melakhah; normally “ein adam choteh velo lo.” Nachalas Shivah end of §2 trends toward forbidding even an intentional beneficiary. For an occasional cook this is nuanced; at a Jewish inn where cooking happens every Shabbat, it is surely forbidden to one who arranged it, and poskim worry about lifnei iver / mesayei le‑devar aveira (Sofer Avraham Chasid §50).
1.יג: For others it is permitted immediately at Motza’ei—we only require “bdei sheyeasu” where the melakhah is performed by a Gentile for a Jew (lest he become careless); where a Jew cooks by hand we do not fear he will openly rely on that example (Beit Yosef, Magen Avraham). If a Gentile boiled water on Shabbat that cooled completely so no benefit accrued from melakhah, some say “bdei sheyeasu” is unnecessary—especially if he drinks it cold; nevertheless same‑day benefit remains rabbinically forbidden (Ateret Zekenim 3). Where cold well‑water must be boiled for safety and then drunk hot, one likely waits Motza’ei “bdei,” since one benefited from the Gentile’s heating.
1.יד: Permitted immediately Motza’ei. If Motza’ei is Yom Tov, it is forbidden—Shabbat does not “prepare” Yom Tov (Likutei Mahari Veil §2; Kenesset HaGedolah Hagahos Taz; Magen Avraham; Ateret Zekenim 3; Teshuvah Me’ahavah 2; Arukh HaShulchan 4—some dispute whether hachanah applies). R”Z 3: same law if food was cooked on Shabbat for an ill person when Motza’ei is Yom Tov—healthy people may not partake. Only applies to items not normally eaten raw (Ateret Zekenim). When Yom Tov falls Monday/Tuesday, Tuesday is permitted (OC 513:5 Hagah). Water cooled before Motza’ei that falls on Yom Tov—no hachanah issue (Ateret Zekenim). Customaries who drink only re‑boiled water may treat reheating as hachanah and forbid drinking that Motza’ei when it is Yom Tov.
1.טו: Same rule—Motza’ei permitted immediately. Rema YD 102 Hagah: if the forbidden portion mixes in, it becomes batel; we do not invoke davar sheyesh lo matirin for someone forbidden forever—therefore bitul applies. Chokhmas Adam disagrees for “others,” since they have matirin after Shabbat—still considered davar sheyesh lo matirin. Magen Avraham 2 forbids the mixture even for the cook that same day because relative to others there are matirin at Motza’ei. Ateret Zekenim 3, R”Z 4—batel brov. Rav Pe’alim I:17 analyses but concludes stringent like Magen Avraham (pattern differs). Ben Ish Hai likewise. R”Z: if mixed on Shabbat the blend stays forbidden to the mezid forever—yet following Rav Pe’alim’s thrust one might equal others; mainstream Rema/Chokhmas Adam leniencies suggest forbidding only that day. Chiddushei R. Akiva Eiger: after Shabbat even the cook is permitted. If Motza’ei is Yom Tov and delay ruins the dish, some permit once batel even shogeg that day (Ateret Zekenim).
1.טז: Shogeg—same‑day prohibition parallels mezid lest people intentionally cook and claim shogeg (R”Z 1).
1.יז: Actions performed on a rav’s mistaken ruling count as shogek and do not trigger penalties (Radbaz bayit 26 II; Kenesset HaGedolah Hagahos Taz; Magen Avraham 3; Ateret Zekenim 5; Teshuvah Me’ahavah 3; R”Z 2).
1.יח: Pure forgetfulness is considered shogeg (Maharam Mintz §28; Kenesset HaGedolah; Magen Avraham; Ateret Zekenim; Teshuvah Me’ahavah; R”Z; Arukh HaShulchan 3—same in his YD §99:10), whether he forgot it was Shabbat or that the act was melakhah.
1.יט: Someone who sincerely thinks it is permitted is treated as shogeg (Magna Avraham OC 104:6; Pitchei Teshuvah there). Arukh HaShulchan notes some dispute but concludes this is ikkar; see OC 253:21.
1.כ: How to compare ones (coercion) to shogeg (R. Binyamin Ze’ev §130; Kenesset HaGedolah; Ateret Zekenim). R. Yonatan: ones is lighter than shogeg because the Torah exempts ones.
1.כא: If one deliberately placed eggs into another’s pot and they cooked: the eggs themselves are forbidden; Kaf HaChayim suggests the stew may be permitted—although eggs are not batel, unpeeled eggs give negligible ta’am (like egg taste in water); analogous to non‑kosher eggs that do not forbid the pot unless peeled or containing blood/chicks (YD 86; see Sha’arei Teshuvah YD 4).
1.כב: See Responsa Zera Ra’anan II §5 about an innkeeper’s Shabbat stew mishap (minor placed pot in oven unaware); lean toward leniency for the stew. Avraham Chasid 3. Rema near end of §1—cross‑reference OC 307:20 Tosafos and §318:19.

2.כג: [SA 2] Sick yesterday or today—Even if the animal fell ill only today (no prior intent), a healthy person may eat its meat and there is no muktzeh concern. Reason (Ra’ash): we follow R. Shimon—muktzeh midde’issura requires two factors (discarded by hand and unsuitable like figs), absent here. Beit David, Beit Yosef, Bach. Fruit still attached after falling—Magna Avraham 4 explains concern is lest one climb and detach (Beitzah), not lest one slaughter—slaughter is burdensome and uncommon.
2.כד: R. Shlomo Luria Chullin ch. 1 §30 forbids when illness began today because of muktzeh. Kenesset HaGedolah Beit Yosef 2; Ateret Zekenim 6.
2.כה: Healthy eaters permitted because obtaining a kezayis of meat requires slaughter, so slaughter is clearly for the ill person (Gemara, Rashi). No gezerah lest one slaughter extra for healthy diners when even the ill portion demands shechitah. Where a small chicken suffices for the patient, larger slaughter—discussed OC 328:16.
2.כו: Permitted to eat raw without salting (Tur). Tosafot and Ra’ash explain salting raw meat would violate mishabein (processing blood). Rinsing removes surface blood but blood absorbed without flowing out is milder (YD 67:1–2; Magna Avraham 5). Rinsing for immediate consumption is permitted on Shabbat (Ateret Zekenim 5).
2.כז: Forbidden on Shabbat for healthy eaters; Magen Avraham permits immediate consumption without waiting Motza’ei “bdei sheyeasu” (Beit Yosef).
2.כח: Muktzeh rules: permitted to move where drinkable; where not drinkable, carrying for others without patient need is forbidden (Yam Shel Shlomo Chullin §30; Kenesset HaGedolah Hagahos Taz 2).
2.כט: Patient without mortal danger: whatever a Jew may not do we decree lest one increase portions because sometimes no Gentile will be available—he might multiply cooking for him (Rashba responsa §914; Beit Yosef).
2.ל: Increasing portions—if he adds before the pot reaches the fire it can still be de’orayta; some say derabbanan (Beit Yosef here and OC 331). Rema/Magen Avraham 6: implications for shevut vs. melakhah when danger absent (see Teshuvah Me’ahavah OC 503:1).
2.לא: Rema: even Gentile cooking—forbidden on Shabbat for healthy eaters (decree lest portions increase). R”Z 5 permits Motza’ei immediately even for healthy—no bishulei nochrim concern (Rema YD 113 Hagahos citing Ra’ah; Shakh YD 113; Nachalas Yaakov). Reason: Gentile cooked le‑heter—no “bdei sheyeasu.” Magen Avraham 7. Taz YD 113:15 cites Rashba (Mishmeret HaBayit): even the patient must wait Motza’ei because of bishulei nochrim—all the more healthy—Ra’ah omitted in SA implies Rema disagrees; many achronim debate (Pri Chadash, Perisha, Maginei Erev, Birkei Yosef, Arukh HaShulchan, Chayei Adam, Birkei Yosef OC here; Ben Ish Hai). Many permit Motza’ei if no bishulei nochrim applies e.g. plain water (Ben Ish Hai).
2.לב: Utensils used by Gentiles for Shabbat cooking where bishulei nochrim applies: Arukh HaShulchan YD 24 leans on Ra’ah—no hagalah needed; Chayei Adam says after Motza’ei they may be used even without hagalah. Chayei Adam kelal 69:16 requires kashering (even cheres triple). Birkei Yosef YD 113:18—lechatchilah stringent; bedieved if cooked before kashering but rov permits food. Ben Ish Hai requires kashering; bedieved rov heter permits pot.
2.לג: Rema (growth): applies only when cooking unfinished; fully cooked foods—no hachanah (Magna Avraham 8; Ateret Zekenim 8; R”Z 10; Teshuvah Me’ahavah 14 disputes Magen Avraham).
2.לד: Muktzeh remains an issue: whatever prepared for patient forbidden to healthy because of muktzeh or “increase” rules—healthy may eat Motza’ei immediately without “bdei,” because “bdei” applies only after chillul Shabbat (shogeg/mezid); when prepared entirely le‑heter and health forbidden only due to muktzeh/increase—no “bdei” (Levush).
2.לה: Gentile cooked medicinal drink for healthy Jew who recovered—may not drink leftover “permitted” portion once healed. If originally made for ill Jew and recovered—permitted. If Jew cooked for patient who recovered—Maharsha permits bedieved but Mechaber’s intent unclear (Nachalas Ben Zion §3; Ukrei Hadat §14 cites Maharif permitting eating when recovered).

3.לו: [SA 3] Like fire‑cooking, derivatives of sun‑heat can violate bishul (Gemara; Magna Avraham 9; Teshuvah Me’ahavah 11). Hence gezerah against solar derivatives.
3.לז: Example: placing egg beside pot—if it reaches ben drusai roasting it is bishul like roasting on flame (R”Z 7). Shiur ben drusai—OC 253:28.
3.לח: Even solar derivatives—dispute R. Yossi vs. rabbis; Rif/Rambam follow rabbis forbidding solar heating (Beit Yosef, Bach). Achronim rule like rabbis; bedieved possibly permitted after Shabbat even for the cook—Gra uncertain.
3.לט: Forbidden to bury on chol hamoed lest one bury in hot ash or dig—Perishah 6; Teshuvah Me’ahavah 15.
3.מ: Same—even intentionally rolling on sand so it roasts is forbidden (Ra’ash, Bach, Magna Avraham 10; R”Z 7). Chiddushei Gra cites Rashba permitting burying mi‑sheini in sand lechatchilah; consensus follows Ra’ash. Rashba responsa §61 permits roasting on sun‑heated roof—not confused with fire‑derivative; Magna Avraham doubts this; Tevu’os Shor argues; Yerushalmi forbids. Netziv/Lechem Mishnah side with Rashba; Magna Avraham/Ateret Zekenim 9; Teshuvah Me’ahavah 14; Nachalas Shivah 6 follow Magna Avraham.
3.מא: Rambam 9:3: cooking in Tiberias hot springs is patur—like solar derivative (Gemara, Mishnah Negaim 9, Sanhedrin 108a regarding flood survivors). Magna Avraham, Teshuvah Me’ahavah, R”Z 8.
3.מב: Ran forbids placing food over Tiberias springs; pouring inside forbidden like OC 326:3. Magna Avraham; Ateret Zekenim; Teshuvah Me’ahavah; R”Z; Gra suggests even fire derivatives may allow shehiyah like cleared stove since no stirring fear.
3.מג: You may not bury even cooked meat in sand mi‑sheini to retain heat—Rashba responsa; Kenesset HaGedolah Hagahos Taz; Ateret Zekenim.
3.מד: Gemara permits lowering stew into cistern for preservation without gezerah of leveling pits—surprised Tur/SA omitted it (Teshuvah Me’ahavah).
3.מה: Direct sunlight differs—unusual for cooking; sun vs. fire not confused, so no gezerah (Ran, Perishah 5; Levush).
3.מו: Sha’arei Zekenim II cites Leket Tov: flame formed by concentrating sunlight through glass is classified as a solar derivative (midrabbanan). Pri To’afos cites this. Lev Chayim III §68 was asked: if one constructs this on Shabbat one violates “do not kindle”; heating/boiling the house or cooking thereby is certainly forbidden; Tal Orot disagrees only for lighting a lamp “from lamp to lamp,” not for substantive heat. If set up erev Shabbat and ignites at sunrise—still forbidden (cited OC 265:1).
3.מז: Rolling an egg on Shabbat in hot lime that is still heated by fire is forbidden. If the lime cooled and was re‑boiled with water after the fire was extinguished, some are lenient—the location never moved, only additional heat from extinguishing (Meiri; Pitchei Teshuvah 19).
3.מח: We hold salted food is like roasted for absorption into vessels, but whether salting counts as “roasting” for Shabbat bishul or for Pesach “roasted” status is disputed (Divrei Chamudot; She’erit Yaakov OC 23). She’erit and Mishnah Berurah 7 infer that cooking after salting can be liable.

4.מט: [SA 4] Know that every rule forbidding bishul includes placing on the stove or in the oven before it was heated (OC 253). Magen Avraham 11; Teshuvah Me’ahavah 16; R”Z 9; Chayei Adam kelal 20:11.
4.נ: Anything involving bishul is forbidden in every form; even if a Gentile cooked it the law matches §1 (Ateret Zekenim 11).
4.נא: Ra’ash and Tur: soup dish that fully cooked and has gravy—if cooled and re‑boiled, bishul applies and one can be liable chatat (Beit Yosef). Rambam 9 writes one who reheats fully cooked food or something needing no cooking is patur—only rabbinic issur; Maggid Mishneh cites Rashba allowing warming opposite a fire without placing on flame even where yad soledes—Beit Yosef infers Ran agrees. This explains Rema below §15 “some are lenient if not completely cooled”; Mishnah Berurah 9; Chayei Adam 20:13—follow communal practice where lenient.
4.נב: There is bishul liability even for toladata ha’or without direct flame. Gemara’s allowance for soaking dry foods from erev in hot water refers to dry foods without gravy (see SA wording nearby). Orchos Chayim 11.
4.נג: Beit Yosef: “yad soledes” defines “boiling”; if after reheating the pot truly boils, one would be exempt only if it had already been yad soledes—implies partial warmth without yad soledes that later reaches boil creates liability (compare Beit Yosef OC 258). Orchos Chayim 12. For yad soledes measurement see §14 below.
4.נד: Once cooled, reheating can involve bishul; if still warm without significant cooling, permitted. Beit Yosef cites Ri ; Magna Avraham 12. Permission applies only to soaking in hot water akin to dry foods near coals where yad soledes (§15)—never on the fire itself (Machatzit HaShekel 2). Hence cooled liquid reheated via keli rishon or fire‑adjacent yad soledes remains problematic.
4.נה: Keli rishon while yad soledes has no “bishul achar bishul”; without yad soledes even keli rishon may regain bishul if reheated to yad soledes. Poured to keli sheni—some say bishul returns if returned to keli rishon (Ateret Zekenim 12).
4.נו: Rema (improves vs. spoils): some say if food softens disadvantageously there is no bishul chatat even after cooling; SA does not distinguish—Bach follows SA (no distinction unless stirring coals issue). Orchos Chayim 13; see §103 below whether SA secretly agrees with Rema regarding softening.
4.נז: Bach on Rema: rejected opinion—softening badly still forbidden. Kenesset HaGedolah Beit Yosef 4; Magen Avraham 13; Levush omitted Rema—some defend Levush via §8; Taz, Magen Avraham 27 and Minchat Kohen recommend stringency unless clearly detrimental (turnips, dates, porridge, fully boiled water); directly on flame always forbidden.
4.נח: Even if already cooked to ben drusai, liability can exist while still boiling—against Ra’ash (who limits chatat until ben drusai), SA follows Tur based on beraita in chapter HaMavi and Rambam (Beit Yosef). Machatzit HaShekel 2 inclines this way.
4.נט: Even ben drusai—but if fully cooked, softening “for the better” involves no further bishul. Orchos Chayim 14; Teshuvah Me’ahavah 19.
4.ס: Regarding foods normally eaten raw: Radbaz ch. I §213 responsum discusses lashes vs. rabbinic prohibition; if fruits cooked on their own from erev they may be eaten. Reasoning: once ben drusai cooking no longer triggers liability for those who eat it that way; certainly raw‑eaten foods differ. Yet where SA holds reheating ben drusai is still bishul (OC 254:4; Rema §14), fruits may still incur liability. Pri Megadim on Levush §62 cites Rivash about beverages vs. vegetables; Mishnah Berurah 6 treats fruits like bishul when flavor changes—debates Radbaz; Birkei Yosef 3 cites Mahari Molcho.
4.סא: Measure of ben drusai—see OC 253:28 and our discussion there.
4.סב: Stew “with gravy” means the majority is liquid (Beit Yosef OC 253 in the name of Ri ; Magen Avraham 11; Minchat Kohen; Mishnah Berurah OC 253:13). Mishnah Berurah OC 259:3 follows majority.
4.סג: Dry food already fully cooked—may soak in hot water as explained in §15 (Teshuvah Me’ahavah 21; R”Z 11; Chayei Adam kelal 20:6).
4.סד: Permitted to soak on Shabbat even if completely cooled until Motza’ei (Teshuvah Me’ahavah 21; R”Z 11; Chayei Adam kelal 20:6).
4.סה: Medicinal “coffee” beverages: major dispute whether stirring roasted powder into cups on Shabbat resembles soaking something never in hot water—Gaon of Ostrog forbids per SA (only rinsing, not soaking); Prague rabbanim permit because powder remains edible dry and travelers eat it that way. Maharam ben Chaviv permits pouring into keli sheni; Maharsha permits but suggests lechatchilah stringency; Maharsha Yitzchaki similar; Maharsha Chiyun permits explicitly. Machatzit HaShekel sides with majority reasoning.
4.סו: Rav Pe’alim III §11 permits pouring coffee-type infusions but discusses coloring/dyeing the water—prefers placing a little coffee erev in water that will be boiled erev so it colors erev; on Shabbat pour that water into a keli sheni then add coffee as needed. Sugar that colors liquids—see §118 below; tie-dye/harina (OC 253:91): if fully cooked/soaked erev one may pour hot water on Shabbat per our siman; strict opinions about “dyeing” liquids may leave no allowance unless water was colored erev.
4.סז: Soaking is permitted, but placing already‑cooked dry food directly on the flame is rabbinically forbidden even without gravy (Rambam); no chatat since fully cooked (Orchos Chayim 16).
4.סח: Soaking even in keli sheni is permitted—no bishul achar bishul for dry foods (§15). Tosafot, Mordekhai, Ran contra Bach. Cannot place keli sheni while still on the fire (§65). Magna Avraham 14; Ateret Zekenim 12; Teshuvah Me’ahavah 21; R”Z 10; Chayei Adam kelal 20:6. “Soaking” implies after removal from fire.
4.סט: If food was only soaked erev but not cooked, soaking Shabbat in hot water may be forbidden if yad soledes—lechatchilah stringent (Magna Avraham). Levush might disagree; practical keli sheni leniency follows Rambam (Ateret Zekenim; Teshuvah Me’ahavah end of 22).
4.ע: Rinsing is permitted—even moist foods—because rinsing is not bishul (Magna Avraham 15; Teshuvah Me’ahavah). Versus soaking distinction.
4.עא: Tosafot (Shabbat 40a): according to Rashba, pouring from keli rishon qualifies as keli sheni—cannot soak but may rinse from keli rishon; according to Rashi, pouring is keli sheni—rinse only from keli sheni. If pouring equals keli rishon, even soaking keli sheni forbidden because resembles cooking (yet spices placed into bowl are permitted—different optics). Bach sides stringently with first explanation—rinse keli sheni only; Yam Shel Sholom 17 follows SA Pesach as pouring keli rishon lechumra; Magna Avraham 15; Ateret Zekenim 13; R”Z 11; Chayei Adam kelal 20:6.
4.עב: Onions are treated like spices “for taste.” Machatzit HaShekel forbids lest they cook; Taz §§8,14 stringent when yad soledes in keli sheni. R”Z permits onions in yad soledes keli sheni like spices (see §106).
4.עג: Old heavily salted fish—Rashi explains “year‑old salty fish”; sailors’ “kuliyas ha’asfanin” eaten via salt must be rinsed—fully restoring them requires bishul and liability if rinsed hot (Gemara). Har haPardes: only if not edible before rinsing; if edible unsalted cold, cold rinse suffices (Orchos Chayim 18). Only cold rinse permitted see next.
4.עד: Cold water rinsing permitted—therefore herring may be rinsed cold even if salty (Beit Yosef citing Har haPardes). Magen Avraham 5; R”Z; Chayei Adam—see following.
4.עה: Rema extends to any tough salted item requiring rinse before eating: only forbidden when impossible without hot water; if edible via cold rinse, hot rinse remains forbidden while cold permitted (Nachalas Binyamin; Ahavas Zekenim difficulty—Kaf HaChayim explains like here). Per this, herring permitted even warm rinse when edible after mild rinse; Taz 5 permits only cold—Machatzit HaShekel 16; Achronim mostly cold only.

5.עו: Rema forbids soaking on Shabbat—R”Z limits prohibition to hot water; cold soaking permitted even if thereby rendered edible (Chayei Adam kelal 20:6 forbids even cold).
5.עז: [SA 5] Ra’am: dry roasted food can undergo further “bishul” after roasting; proof from matzah sheniah and Pesach “bishul after tzli” liability (see Beit Yosef). Ra’avya disputes—matzah unique; Pesach from verse “uvishal.” Even Ra’am would forbid reheating dry roast still hot from roasting just like Pesach law.
5.עח: Rosh: even Ra’am forbids afiyah after afiyah or tzli after tzli (Tur). Beit Yosef agrees—no afiyah after afiyah / tzli after tzli.
5.עט: There is tzli after bishul—therefore dry cooked food near fire without gravy is forbidden (Piskei Ridbaz citing Ra’am and Semag). Orach Latzadik §6: only bare roast near flame without pot; inside pot single “bishul.” Changing roasting style (crisping sliced bread) forbidden—new melakhah/taste (Taz §6). Maḥaneh Leviyah §7: may not place stale bread in hot oven merely to soften—tikkun.
5.פ: While tzli after tzli permits placing near fire when yad soledes location (but soaking hot water forbidden per SA understanding). Never on fire itself (Ateret Zekenim 17; R”Z 13). Coffee dust question referenced earlier (§80).
5.פא: Bread in keli sheni forbidden to those who hold bishul after afiyah because bread softens easily (Orchos Chayim 20).
5.פב: Rema warns other delicate foods—be cautious placing milk or eggs into coffee while keli sheni is yad soledes because they cook quickly (Chayei Adam kelal 20:21; OC 321:15).
5.פג: Those who permit keli sheni follow Tur—only moist salt has alternate definition (Taz §7; Magna Avraham 19). According to §4 Tosafos first answer should be stringent for optics; lenient opinion follows Tosafos second answer—SA practice tends stringent (Magna Avraham).
5.פד: Common practice pouring gravy over bread chunks—Ra’am forbids; communities rely on dissenters permitting keli sheni (perhaps keli rishon—Nachalas Yaakov). Maharshal Hagahos Magen Avraham brought stringent opinion first then lenient—some say final opinion prevails (Nachalas Yaakov Hagahos Taz). Best practice: pour soup first or wait until no longer yad soledes (Machatzit HaShekel 3). Machatzit HaShekel §19 argues SA’s “those who permit” includes keli rishon—worldwide practice dunking bread from tureen supports Ra’avya-like leniency.
5.פה: Rema allows leniency even keli rishon—those equating bishul after bishul with bishul after afiyah for cooled bread. Nevertheless pour soup first or wait until not yad soledes lechatchilah (Nachalas Yaakov; Orchos Chayim 21; Minchat Kohen).
5.פו: Ashkenaz custom avoids placing bread directly into salty cholent—slice onions fine only after gravy cooled below yad soledes; onions might behave like “moist salt” second definition (§9). Taz §§8,14; Tosafos §38 disputes Taz—many lenient onions (see §71); bread leniencies noted above.

6.פז: [SA 6] Hot vessel food not fully cooked cannot be insulated even where heating fully cooked food would be permitted (§4)—here completion remains possible (Taz §9; Ateret Zekenim 20; R”Z 14). Yam Shel Sholom 23 argues unfinished cooking always forbidden as bishul; Mishnah Berurah 9–11 disagrees with Yam Shel Sholom; Ma’amar Mordekhai allows ben drusai finished food even if improves via insulation.
6.פח: Covering pot with blankets when Hatmana permitted—may cover vessel beneath blankets together with permitted hatmana because insulation aims at pot (Machatzit HaShekel 51).
6.פט: May seal lid with dough when dough needed for chickens—not muktzeh (Teshuvah Me’ahavah 27; Ateret Zekenim 22).
6.צ: Smooth paste differs—generally forbidden smearing (OC 314:11); Taz §10 equates thick dough to wax smearing unless minimal dab merely veiling opening (Ateret Zekenim 19; Teshuvah Me’ahavah).
6.צא: “Not very hot” follows SA §4—Rema §15 permits anything not completely cooled (Teshuvah Me’ahavah 28).
6.צג: Dry foods—even completely cooled—permitted except hatmana rules (OC 253:5) (Magna Avraham 23; Ateret Zekenim 23; R”Z 11).
6.צד: Upper vessel whose contents could reach yad soledes—even intent only to warm—forbidden if location allows boiling (Orchos Chayim 24).

7.צה: [SA 7] Lower vessel on fire permitted—pot interrupts direct stove contact like warming near flame (Taz §11; Ateret Zekenim 21; Teshuvah Me’ahavah 29). Machatzit HaShekel §24 cites Yam Shel Sholom §87 unfinished cooking issue.
7.צו: Upper vessel always forbidden—like placing directly on stove lest stir coals (Ri ; OC 253:2 Hagahos). Machatzit HaShekel 24.
7.צז: First opinion is ikkar like §8—Ma’amar Mordekhai and Gra agree.

8.צח: [SA 8] Anything permitted under §4 without bishul—even dry cooled food soaking keli rishon—may sit near coals without stirring worry (Levush).
8.צט: Urinating vessel (“Mayham”) atop kettle on fire—some forbid as if on stove (Machatzit HaShekel 4). Pouring inside kettle on flame—forbidden to all.
8.ק: Some forbid even without bishul lest stir coals (Magna Avraham 21).
8.קא: First reason primary—pot interrupts direct kirah contact (Machatzit HaShekel 26). Machatzit HaShekel critiques wording—yet §253:5 Hagahos cleared kirah issue.
8.קב: Gravy dishes—majority Achronim differentiate liquids despite Rambam/Ran uniform rule (Machatzit HaShekel 5; Ateret Zekenim 27).
8.קג: Softening “for better taste” forbidden near flame unless §15 criteria—Magna Avraham connects Rema §§4 and 15; Minchat Kohen (“third condition”) requires improvement plus yad soledes; examine §§56–57.

9.קד: [SA 9] Keli rishon while yad soledes cooks any time; keli sheni—even yad soledes—does not cook because walls lack retained heat (Beit Yosef; YD 105:2).
9.קה: If no yad soledes, placing food is permitted despite minority stringent opinions about absorption (Tehilah leDavid kelal 57). Yerushalmi/Teshuvot Beitzah distance keli rishon near fire even without yad soledes—Achronim mostly lenient when not yad soledes near flame (Shakh YD 105:5; Pri Chadash YD 108 §§10,22; Gra). Rivash debated Shakh but consensus follows lenient Achronim except individuals who choose stringency.
9.קו: Salt—Gemara records two readings; Rif/Rambam/Ra’ash follow lenient second reading; Tosafot praise stringent first opinion (Beit Yosef). Rema quotes “some forbid” even keli sheni—SA omitted stringent view; Gra praises kabbalistic stringency.
9.קז: Once removed from fire obvious—cannot return while on flame (Beit Yosef citing Ran).
9.קח: Some forbid salty meat in vessel—moisture cooks quickly despite needing “much cooking” (Tur)—Ra’ash singular opinion recorded because SA records uncommon opinions when labeled.
9.קט: Even unsalted meat—moisture cooks per Tur; Bach follows Rema even without external salt (Teshuvah Me’ahavah 36).
9.קי: Rema blood concern—after salting one rinsed blood—otherwise blood-in-salt issue persists (YD 69:9).
9.קיא: “Some forbid salt”—because salt cooks even keli sheni (Orchos Chayim 29; see §106).
9.קיב: Rema: salt nullifies into food—not davar sheyesh lo matirin after Shabbat because salt itself never “cooks” alone—it seasons meat like yeast mixture cases where both contribute (Shaarei Dura cited Beit Yosef). Taz disputes—requires simultaneous cooperative causation; nevertheless Achronim largely permit Rema’s reasoning (see Pri Megadim YD Shaar HaTaroves VII).
9.קיג: Salt poured now must lack standalone shiur to forbid—otherwise forbidden like YD §§87, Orlah mishnah (Magna Avraham; Achronim).
9.קיד: Mordekhai/Kolbo: modern refined salt cooked during processing—Machmir since “everything entering hot water erev…” yet “those stringent praised” (Darchei Moshe 4; Magna Avraham).

10.קטו: [SA 10] Spices may not be placed then havdalah poured—Chazal hold pouring keli rishon equals keli rishon lechumra but lenient for kashering iruy (Taz §16).
10.קטז: If poured first, peels forbidden—cooked Shabbat (Magna Avraham 32; Ateret Zekenim 25; Teshuvah Me’ahavah 40; R”Z 19). Keli sheni never cooks leketzin—even absorption debates irrelevant for melakhah definitions.
10.קיז: Pour keli rishon into bowl first, then spices—keli sheni cannot cook even when yad soledes (R”Z 19; Ben Ish Hai Beshalach 9).
10.קיח: Pouring havdalah brew onto sugar in cups—Pan Meirot permits; Zechor laAvraham OC 14 hesitates—prefer sugar first then liquid (Machatzit HaShekel 3; She’eilat Yaakov 28; Chayei Adam kelal 20:7). Only applies to boiling keli rishon yad soledes (She’eilat Yaakov).

11.קיט: [SA 11] Bathtub fed hot spring—even Tiberias water—may not pour cold inside; take water with keli sheni then add (Gemara; Nachalas Shiva 33; Ateret Zekenim 26).
11.קכ: Spring-fed pit retains keli rishon status even after disconnect—may not float oil flask atop surface even with separator; pouring into Tiberias-heated keli sheni permitted. If heated by fire for bathing—different rules (Ateret Zekenim 33).
11.קכא: Rema: even keli sheni bathing tubs—water is usually scalding so added cold water is negligible (Tur). Machatzit HaShekel 34; R”Z 20.
11.קכב: Pouring hot into abundant cold—even from keli rishon—is permitted because “tata’ah gavar” (bottom dominates); unlike spices (§15), here liquids mix and chill. Do not drop a boiling chunk of meat into cold sauce lest it cooks locally (YD 91:4; Pesachim 76; Magen Avraham 35; Ateret Zekenim 28; Teshuvah Me’ahavah end 41; R”Z 20).

12.קכד: May add abundant cold water; may not add a small amount lest it heats to yad soledes (Tur). R”Z 21.
12.קכה: Majority cold water—we do not say the vessel “combines temperatures” when unintended and not pesik reisha (Magna Avraham 36; Ateret Zekenim 30; Teshuvah Me’ahavah 42).
12.קכו: Maggid Mishneh: unintended temperature mixing is not pesik reisha melakhah—parallel toothpick trimming not for tooth‑cleaning (OC 322:4); dispute whether liable for unintended tzoref derabbanan/de’oraita (Magna Avraham; Ateret Zekenim; Teshuvah Me’ahavah).
12.קכז: “To thaw”—warming to comfortable drinking is forbidden (yad soledes); hence urn bathwater heating—even merely defrosting—is stricter than ordinary warming (Orchos Chayim 34).
12.קכח: Pouring from keli sheni permitted—keli sheni does not cook (Orchos Chayim 35). Even small cold mixed with pour reaching yad soledes permitted since keli sheni cannot cook (see §§104, 117).
12.קכט: Cold into hot—should be one continuous pour; dribbling bit-by-bit forbidden because immediate localized cooking occurs (Chayei Adam kelal 20:3 resolves Bach difficulty; Ben Ish Hai Beshalach 11).
12.קל: Rema limits: only when contents not on fire; cold into hot permitted even on keli rishon when lower cold dominates and majority cold cannot reach yad soledes (Orchos Chayim 36; Teshuvah Me’ahavah 44).
12.קלא: Hagahos: must be impossible for foods to reach full boil—only removing chill.
12.קלב: Hagahos: even keli rishon permitted; cold into hot requires large single pour (Levush; see §129).
12.קלג: Hagahos: must not be on fire nor adjacent where food could reach yad soledes—see §14.

13.קלד: [SA 13] Keli sheni cannot cook even when yad soledes because walls lack residual heat (Beit Yosef citing Tosafot; Orchos Chayim 38).
13.קלה: Drawing with empty cup from keli rishon—Taz YD 92 (and here §19) stringent: treated like keli rishon; if liquid sat inside until boiling certainly keli rishon (Ateret Zekenim 32; Teshuvah Me’ahavah 6–7).
13.קלו: May not bury entire flask inside keli sheni (hatmana)—mouth must protrude (Taz §19). R”Z 23 permits complete immersion; see OC 258:2.
13.קלז: Hamudi Daniel / Pitchei Teshuvah: spring-fed bathtub discussed §11—even keli sheni flask may be forbidden there.
13.קלח: Keli rishon forbidden—even merely removing chill—gezerah lest one forget and leave until yad soledes; same for Tiberias-fed tubs—lift with keli sheni then immerse (R”Z 23; see §119).
13.קלט: Unless upper cold volume so dominant cooking impossible—like interrupted mixer case (Beit Me’ir).

14.קמ: [SA 14] Opposite flame lit by Gentile for himself or Jew because of cold—permitted area (Chayei Adam kelal 20:11).
14.קמא: Removing chill—even fully thawing permitted where yad soledes impossible (Tosafot Shabbat 48b “mai”; Beit Yosef).
14.קמב: Even if staying long time without reaching yad soledes—permitted (R”Z 24).
14.קמג: Practical gauge: if liquid comfortably drinkable/eatable because heat—below threshold; if too hot to drink/eat—yad soledes region (Ben Ish Hai Beshalach 5).
14.קמד: Even brief placement forbidden near flame where food could finish cooking—Ra’ash-style concern one may extend stay until boiling; differs from Rambam/Rashi (Orchos Chayim 44).
14.קמה: Rema: same for fruit—even raw-edible fruit—may not approach fire to remove chill where boiling possible (Orchos Chayim 40; see §60). Farther away permitted even foods not eaten raw. Wax tablets (“aluntit”) or lead vessels near fire to warm—if melting possible—Magna Avraham 37 debates davar she’ein mitkaven; alternative reasoning: fear of forgetting removal—less concern before melting (Teshuvah Me’ahavah 47).

15.קמו: [SA 15] Fully cooked dry food—may place near heat if no yad soledes zone; unfinished—even ben drusai/roasting—may not be positioned where yad soledes attainable (Beit Yosef; Orchos Chayim 41).
15.קמז: Persian custom warming stuffed chickens/melianash inside oven Shabbat morning—permitted without gravy; side-opening oven resembles warming near coals more than direct flame (Maharimat responsa §10; Birkei Yosef 4; Mayim Rabim §21 permit leaning toward oven with slight solid fat but forbid abundant soup because tzimutz occurs; oven insertion might resemble cooking even after done—Machatzit HaShekel 35 notes lenient customs).
15.קמח: May place cooked coffee infusion opposite coals even if Jew prepared; may not place on fire—even Gentile or automatic feet igniter questionable (Kenesset HaGedolah responsa §102; Birkei Yosef 5; Machatzit HaShekel there; Zechor laMiriam 2 disputes Kenesset HaGedolah vs. Kol Eliyahu §14; see OC 253:11).
15.קמט: Opposite coals permitted—no normal “cooking path”; on fire forbidden—Maharil/Eliyyahu Hagahos; Birkei Yosef Shiyurei Berachah 3—because some hold bishul achar bishul / after tzli exists.
15.קנ: This entire paragraph treats §4 dry foods without bishul: still may not sit on kirah because of stirring fear, yet near coals permitted like leaning on kirah for reasons Magen Avraham explained (Levush). See following.
15.קנא: Near coals resembles leaning on permitted kirah—no separator needed since slight distance gives recognition and prevents stirring (Ra’ash; Magna Avraham 38; Teshuvah Me’ahavah 48).
15.קנב: Even where yad soledes exists—dry foods lack bishul achar bishul (§4) (Teshuvah Me’ahavah 49).
15.קנג: Rema: even with gravy once fully cooked—(Orchos Chayim 42).
15.קנד: Rema: even after cooling—those without bishul achar bishul for liquids permit (Magna Avraham 14; Ateret Zekenim 35; Teshuvah Me’ahavah 50; see §51).
15.קנה: Custom lenient if still warm; if cooled beyond edibility looks like repair—forbidden (Ateret Zekenim 44). If goal merely slight warming (not yad soledes), some permit even fully cooled without gezerah—yet must guard against leaving until boil (Chayei Adam kelal 20:13).

16.קנו: [SA 16] May place “infida” (pastry dough pocket filled with fat—Perishah 11; later Poskim).
16.קנז: Rambam/Rashi/R. Y Feriershom: unlike crushing ice/snow for liquid (OC 320:9 gezerah sechitah), passive warming opposite fire/sun is not nolad because snow retains beverage status; Rashba agrees (Orchos Chayim 43; Beit Yosef).
16.קנח: Levush questioned placing near fire where yad soledes—thought oil resembles oil heating (§15). Magna Avraham rejects comparison—dry cooked pocket lacks bishul (§15; OC 253:5); Gemara/Rashi/Shabbat 145; Mordekhai; Hagahos Semag; Minchat Kohen agree. Perishah rejects Levush; Teshuvah Me’ahavah 51; Birkei Yosef 6; Achronim. If fat leaks outward see §163 stringent opinions about nolad.
16.קנט: Rema: stew with gravy—solid fat dissolves unnoticeably into soup like OC 320:9 allowance pouring into bowl because unrecognizable when melted (Orchos Chayim 45).
16.קס: Rema continuation: yet stringent opinions (§15 dry-only rule) forbid true yad soledes improvement—Machatzit HaShekel 41. Levush explains Rema’s “even stew” discussing nolad leniency where no yad soledes; true yad soledes remains bishul (Teshuvah Me’ahavah 52).
16.קסא: Solidified gravy floating fat becomes “new liquid” when melted—even without yad soledes according to some—unless only fat congealed atop liquid while broth stayed liquid (Minchat Fetem).
16.קסב: Stringent poskim: fat recognizable floating differs from snow dissolving entirely—even solar melting forbidden (Orchos Chayim 46).
16.קסג: Further stringency: fat rises visibly—nolad resembling squeezed juice; unlike snow melting invisibly (OC 320:9). Bedieved oil may re-enter pastry—YD 113:3—but lenient bedieved like Rema. Lechatchilah place pastry before oven heated—like OC 253:3—even bedieved some permit before heating; public leniency should use Gentile if possible (Magna Avraham 42; Ateret Zekenim 36; Teshuvah Me’ahavah 53; Chayei Adam kelal 20:20; caution fish jellied gravy—Machatzit HaShekel). Pri Megadim 4 disputes Magna Avraham’s strict bedieved fat consumption; permits even yad soledes bedieved; without yad soledes lechatchilah permitted—Machatzit HaShekel 44 cites mistaken strict customs.
16.קסד: Ba’al haTurim: if poured liquids/fat out erev Shabbat—may reheat pastry Shabbat; Bach infers even stringent view permits reheating fatty meat chunks if minority moisture—because minimal melting insignificant (Taz §21; Ateret Zekenim; Teshuvah Me’ahavah).
16.קסה: Dirshu Maharash: wine flask filled with ice may sit on oven to melt ice—wine hides ice (Ateret Zekenim). Same requires non‑boiling spot (§14); some forbid “bishul” in wine generally (see §60).
16.קסו: Hagahos: rely on first reasoning; Bach concurs; Achronim agree.

17.קסז: [SA 17] Following Rema §15 leniency for not fully cooled foods—same here if fully cooked and still somewhat warm.
17.קסח: Long placement forbidden lest one forget until fully cooked (Teshuvah Me’ahavah 54; Levush).
17.קסט: Same law as opposite coals—no stirring concern per §15 (Teshuvah Me’ahavah 55; Levush).
17.קע: If food not very hot—permitted; even if cold item never cooked (see §175).

18.קעא: [SA 18] Boiling pot removed—stirring (“hagasah”) obligation chatat; some say only first stir counts before rapid cooking; afterward stirring exempt—Ramban/Rashba; Maggid Mishneh 9:4; Beit Yosef; Magna Avraham 42. Possibly even off fire if unfinished—but Beit Yosef OC 253 cites Kalebo that stirring finished pot on fire still bishul—Machatzit HaShekel; Teshuvah Me’ahavah 56.
18.קעב: Added case off fire while still boiling—certainly unfinished cooking forbidden.
18.קעג: If unfinished—may not stir; if finished while still on fire—Beit Yosef cites Maggid Mishneh permitting inserting spoon and removing food (Bach OC 252). Ateret Zekenim 44 balances opinions; Otzar 40 concludes on-fire removal forbidden; Chayei Adam kelal 20:9—see Rema below.
18.קעד: Italian stew fully cooked erev Shabbat left by Gentile Friday night near fire—some rely on wooden spatula to reposition before ladling cups (Zechor laAvraham OC 40; Machatzit HaShekel 6; OC 321:19).
18.קעה: Large sequential meals Friday night—pots stay on stove; permitted to shovel coals even if coals not ash-covered and stirring rotates food toward heat—Radbaz (Piove di Sacco) III §111; Machatzit HaShekel 7.
18.קעו: Wool dyebath—coloring concern plus lengthy cooking (Ra’ash; Taz §22). Teshuvah Me’ahavah 57 says SA primary concern is bishul, not dye alone—Machatzit HaShekel imprecise.
18.קעז: Rema: lechatchilah caution with beans removed by spoon—since unavoidable, lenient customs rely on opinions (Magna Avraham 44). Taz §23: once finished cooking no hagasah issue—only forbid rotating pot if possible pour instead; world lenient removing lentil stew off fire with spoon when finished—still stir while yad soledes should pour if easy (R”Z 30; OC 321:19).

19.קעח: [SA 19] While opposite coals—or removed from fire while yad soledes—may not smear fat/garlic on roast (still keli rishon per §§9, Taz §24; Magna Avraham 45; Teshuvah Me’ahavah 59). Many unknowingly smear garlic on hot roast—forbidden when yad soledes. If smeared—requires peeling width garlic thickness + finger oil until sixty (Mishnah Berurah 24); thick solids—even keli sheni might cook (Pri Megadim YD 105; roast a fortiori). Bedieved lenient—keli sheni often doesn’t cook (Mishnah Berurah).
19.קעט: Fat without garlic—Kaf HaChayim thinks permitted—no bishul or nolad when not recognizable (§16); sprinkle gradually melts—perhaps “recognizable” like gravy pot—uncertain (Magna Avraham; Ateret Zekenim 41 leniencies; R”Z 28 compares fatty stew crust—common stringency lechatchilah; bedieved lenient when needed).
19.קפ: Garlic still cooks—yet proof for smearing poultry schmaltz onto grains/kasha/lokshen bowls Shabbat: even visible melt entering food may be permitted since no independent cooking on surface—only absorption (Derishah 6; Ateret Zekenim; R”Z—Achronim permit).
